paper.title: World Models Need Not Be Right to Rank Policies Right: Relative Bounds and Audit Limits
paper.abstract: Abstract Selecting a reinforcement-learning (RL) policy usually requires additional environment interaction, while learned world models offer cheap but potentially biased evaluations. This raises two distinct questions: can shared model errors preserve pairwise rankings despite poor absolute values, and do they make a small number of real audits more informative? We derive an exact pairwise simulation identity and a relative bound separating common-mode Bellman residuals from policy-specific error. The analysis motivates RAVEL (Relative Auditing of Value Errors in Learned models), a selective policy tournament whose eliminations use held-out real outcomes. We test 45 SAC, TD3, and PPO policies per task in DMC cheetah-run and walker-walk. At rollout horizon 500, model rankings remain strong (Kendall τ = 0.962 \tau=0.962 and 0.800 0.800 ), and same-run differential-error ratios are 0.674 0.674 and 0.106 0.106 . Yet mean paired audit-error correlations are only 0.007 0.007 and 0.090 0.090 , and pairing changes standard deviation by − 2.5 % -2.5\% and + 1.9 % +1.9\% . Simultaneous intervals attain 99.98 % 99.98\% and 99.75 % 99.75\% coverage, but certify only 13.2 % 13.2\% and 0 % 0\% of decisions at eight audits. RAVEL improves low-budget walker-walk regret, whereas real-only successive halving is better at the largest budget, rejecting the precommitted twofold efficiency target. Frozen-model optimization lowers real return without increasing predicted return on average. Thus ranking fidelity, useful audit covariance, and upward model exploitation are distinct properties, separated in part by closed-loop trajectory divergence.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reinforcement learning (RL) has no direct analogue of a supervised validation set. Choosing a checkpoint, seed, algorithm, or hyperparameter setting normally requires additional environment interaction. Off-policy evaluation (OPE) addresses this problem from logged data, but accurate value estimation is difficult under policy-induced distribution shift [ 18 , 8 , 4 ] . Modern world models offer another route: freeze a learned simulator, roll each candidate policy out inside it, and use the resulting return as a cheap validation score. This use case is no longer hypothetical. WorldEval, WorldGym, and related video-world-model studies report meaningful correlation between simulated and physical policy performance, including preservation of some checkpoint and model rankings [ 10 , 15 , 19 ] . A decision-making-centric evaluation proposal consequently places policy ranking near the top of the evidence ladder for useful world models [ 21 ] . Yet two issues remain. First, current evaluations emphasize global statistics such as Pearson correlation or average rank violations. Model selection applies an arg ⁡ max \arg\max : among many candidates it chooses the one with the largest predicted value. Increasing the candidate pool increases the opportunity to select an unusually positive model error. High average correlation can therefore coexist with poor top-1 selection. This is a sequential-decision instance of the optimizer’s curse [ 17 ] ; recent work formalizes both ordinal model exploitation in RL [ 2 ] and the selection tax for general surrogate-assisted search [ 13 ] . Second, standard simulation bounds control each policy’s absolute value error separately. They can be unnecessarily pessimistic for ranking. If a model underestimates every policy by the same amount, its absolute error may be large while every pairwise order is exact. Ranking depends on the difference between two model biases, not their sum. The relevant scientific question is thus: When can an inaccurate world model nevertheless provide a reliable policy ranking, and how much real interaction is needed to discover when it cannot? We make four contributions. 1. An exact pairwise simulation identity and a relative residual/occupancy bound for ranking and top-1 regret certificates. 2. RAVEL, which orders comparisons with model rollouts but certifies eliminations only with held-out real outcomes. 3. A controlled study separating expected-bias cancellation from finite-sample audit covariance. 4. Evidence that strong rankings need not make matched audits informative at horizon 500. Equation (2) subtracts two standard simulation identities, and (5) is an elementary triangle-inequality bound; neither step is claimed as a new lemma. Our contribution is the explicit common-residual/occupancy decomposition, its ranking certificates, and evidence that expected-error cancellation need not yield audit savings.

sections.heading: World models and evaluation.
sections.text: DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 use learned dynamics primarily for policy improvement [ 5 , 6 ] ; compounding error motivates short or conservative model use [ 7 , 16 ] . WorldEval, WorldGym, and related video-model studies instead evaluate policies and report partial agreement with real rankings [ 10 , 15 , 19 ] , but do not give a ranking-specific simulation decomposition or candidate-pool stress test.

sections.heading: Policy selection and confidence.
sections.text: OPE estimates values from logged data, including doubly robust estimators [ 8 ] . OPCC benchmarks offline pairwise confidence and model-based baselines on logged data [ 9 ] ; we do not claim pairwise confidence or model-based comparison as new. We rank fixed policies from frozen world-model rollouts and correct scores with held-out real outcomes. Liu et al. study OPE-model-selection tournaments [ 11 ] , while proxy-assisted best-arm methods use correlated predictions as controls [ 14 ] . RAVEL is not a generic new tournament: it focuses on a world-model residual/occupancy bound and whether matched errors reduce audit variance. Surrogate methods also require true-data certification [ 13 ] .

sections.heading: Relative error.
sections.text: Bhamidipaty et al. characterize ordinal inversions in imperfect world models [ 2 ] . Counterfactual quotient models remove action-independent shared future components while preserving action comparisons [ 3 ] ; our setting instead concerns fixed-policy return ranking under policy-dependent occupancies and real-audit certification. Classical simulation lemmas bound absolute value error [ 12 ] , while cancellation can aid cross-validation even when absolute risk is inaccurate [ 20 ] .

sections.heading: 5.2 Procedure
sections.text: RAVEL first orders all policies with cheap model rollouts, but never eliminates from model score alone. It audits consequential champion–challenger pairs on fresh conditions, adaptively eliminates only when a real-data lower confidence bound is positive, and returns either a globally certified singleton or an unresolved/shortlist-conditional set. Audit outcomes remain held out from model and policy training. RAVEL-U uses unpaired per-policy intervals; RAVEL-P uses matched pairwise intervals. sections.heading: 6.1 Design and implementation
sections.text: We evaluate DMC cheetah-run and walker-walk at horizon 500. For each task, SAC, TD3, and PPO are trained under three seeds for 10 6 10^{6} environment steps; five checkpoints per run give 45 policies. A five-member probabilistic dynamics ensemble is fitted to 5 × 10 5 5\times 10^{5} pooled transitions. Each policy receives 128 imagined rollouts and 50 held-out environment episodes. The analysis contains all 990 unordered pairs, and samples 200 candidate pools at each K ∈ { 8 , 16 , 32 } K\in\{8,16,32\} with audit budgets n ∈ { 0 , 2 , 4 , 8 } n\in\{0,2,4,8\} . Audit outcomes are not used for model or policy training. Each task requires fitting a five-member ensemble on 5 × 10 5 5\times 10^{5} transitions and up to 45 × 128 × 500 = 2.88 × 10 6 45\times 128\times 500=2.88\times 10^{6} imagined model steps, plus 50 held-out episodes per policy. We did not record wall-clock or energy cost; these counts contextualize the two-task scope but do not quantify its compute burden or imply runtime savings. The supplied run record reports completion without failed stages on PyTorch 2.3.1/CUDA 12.1 using MuJoCo EGL. Matching was checked by resetting every policy from the same stored seed list. A synthetic unit test is not treated as empirical evidence: it injects shared-noise SD 20 and policy-noise SD 2, making correlation 0.99 by construction. For one logged cheetah SAC run, training return rose from 44.5 to 653.0; the cheetah dynamics holdout MSE fell from 0.961 to a best value of 0.125. Analysis-time returns use a different finite-horizon scale, so all comparisons below use only the common analysis definition. sections.heading: 6.4 Frozen-model stress test
sections.text: Ten policies per task receive 500 additional gradient steps against the frozen model. The resulting inversion rates are 0.30 and 0.20, and mean real-return losses are 22.43 and 28.50 for cheetah-run and walker-walk. However, mean model-return changes are also negative, − 4.56 -4.56 and − 17.45 -17.45 . This is not the canonical case in which an optimizer drives predicted reward upward while true reward falls. It is a model-blind collapse: degradation in the environment is substantially larger than, and sometimes invisible to, the model. One cheetah TD3 checkpoint changes from 328.8 to 150.0 in the environment while its model score changes only from 371.6 to 372.9. Detection at n = 2 n=2 and n = 4 n=4 is 0% on both tasks. At n = 8 n=8 , detection reaches 66.7% on cheetah-run and remains 0% on walker-walk. Thus this stress test supplies evidence of consequential ordinal failure but not of systematic upward model exploitation.

sections.heading: Three notions of correctness.
sections.text: We distinguish absolute calibration ( J ^ i ≈ J i \widehat{J}_{i}\approx J_{i} ), ordinal utility (correct differences and selections), and audit utility (correlated errors that make small audits informative). The first is unnecessary for the second, and at horizon 500 the second does not imply the third. Evaluation should therefore report differential error and top-policy regret together with audit covariance, coverage, and abstention.

sections.heading: 7 Limitations and Scope
sections.text: The identity is exact under the stated Markov/shared-state assumptions, but certificates still require representative audits, bounded errors, and finite-rollout uncertainty; RAVEL cannot remove support mismatch. We study two state-based tasks, one horizon-500 suite per task, overlapping pools from 45 policies, and estimated 50-episode references, so the results establish conditional rather than independent-run generalization. Short horizons, smaller evaluator datasets, latent models, and robots remain untested. The compute counts above do not include wall-clock or energy measurements. The stress test shows degradation rather than systematic upward exploitation [ 2 ] , and universal proxy savings are impossible [ 14 , 13 ] .

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: World models can preserve rankings while remaining poor audit control variates. At horizon 500, RAVEL is safe but indecisive; ranking, calibration, and audit utility must be evaluated separately.

This raises two distinct questions: can shared model errors preserve pairwise rankings despite poor absolute values, and do they make a small number of real audits more informative? We derive an exact pairwise simulation identity and a relative bound separating common-mode Bellman residuals from policy-specific error. The analysis motivates RAVEL (Relative Auditing of Value Errors in Learned models), a selective policy tournament whose eliminations use held-out real outcomes. We test 45 SAC, TD3, and PPO policies per task in DMC cheetah-run and walker-walk. At rollout horizon 500, model rankings remain strong (Kendall τ = 0.962 \tau=0.962 and 0.800 0.800 ), and same-run differential-error ratios are 0.674 0.674 and 0.106 0.106 . Yet mean paired audit-error correlations are only 0.007 0.007 and 0.090 0.090 , and pairing changes standard deviation by − 2.5 % -2.5\% and + 1.9 % +1.9\% . Simultaneous intervals attain 99.98 % 99.98\% and 99.75 % 99.75\% coverage, but certify only 13.2 % 13.2\% and 0 % 0\% of decisions at eight audits. RAVEL improves low-budget walker-walk regret, whereas real-only successive halving is better at the largest budget, rejecting the precommitted twofold efficiency target. Thus ranking fidelity, useful audit covariance, and upward model exploitation are distinct properties, separated in part by closed-loop trajectory divergence. A Preprint 1 Introduction Reinforcement learning (RL) has no direct analogue of a supervised validation set. Choosing a checkpoint, seed, algorithm, or hyperparameter setting normally requires additional environment interaction. Off-policy evaluation (OPE) addresses this problem from logged data, but accurate value estimation is difficult under policy-induced distribution shift [ 18 , 8 , 4 ] . Modern world models offer another route: freeze a learned simulator, roll each candidate policy out inside it, and use the resulting return as a cheap validation score. This use case is no longer hypothetical. WorldEval, WorldGym, and related video-world-model studies report meaningful correlation between simulated and physical policy performance, including preservation of some checkpoint and model rankings [ 10 , 15 , 19 ] . A decision-making-centric evaluation proposal consequently places policy ranking near the top of the evidence ladder for useful world models [ 21 ] . Yet two issues remain. First, current evaluations emphasize global statistics such as Pearson correlation or average rank violations. Model selection applies an arg ⁡ max \arg\max : among many candidates it chooses the one with the largest predicted value. Increasing the candidate pool increases the opportunity to select an unusually positive model error. High average correlation can therefore coexist with poor top-1 selection. This is a sequential-decision instance of the optimizer’s curse [ 17 ] ; recent work formalizes both ordinal model exploitation in RL [ 2 ] and the selection tax for general surrogate-assisted search [ 13 ] . Second, standard simulation bounds control each policy’s absolute value error separately. They can be unnecessarily pessimistic for ranking. If a model underestimates every policy by the same amount, its absolute error may be large while every pairwise order is exact. Ranking depends on the difference between two model biases, not their sum. The relevant scientific question is thus: When can an inaccurate world model nevertheless provide a reliable policy ranking, and how much real interaction is needed to discover when it cannot? We make four contributions. 1. An exact pairwise simulation identity and a relative residual/occupancy bound for ranking and top-1 regret certificates. 2. RAVEL, which orders comparisons with model rollouts but certifies eliminations only with held-out real outcomes. 3. A controlled study separating expected-bias cancellation from finite-sample audit covariance. 4. Evidence that strong rankings need not make matched audits informative at horizon 500. Equation (2) subtracts two standard simulation identities, and (5) is an elementary triangle-inequality bound; neither step is claimed as a new lemma. Our contribution is the explicit common-residual/occupancy decomposition, its ranking certificates, and evidence that expected-error cancellation need not yield audit savings. 2 Related Work World models and evaluation. DreamerV3 and TD-MPC2 use learned dynamics primarily for policy improvement [ 5 , 6 ] ; compounding error motivates short or conservative model use [ 7 , 16 ] . WorldEval, WorldGym, and related video-model studies instead evaluate policies and report partial agreement with real rankings [ 10 , 15 , 19 ] , but do not give a ranking-specific simulation decomposition or candidate-pool stress test. OPCC benchmarks offline pairwise confidence and model-based baselines on logged data [ 9 ] ; we do not claim pairwise confidence or model-based comparison as new. We rank fixed policies from frozen world-model rollouts and correct scores with held-out real outcomes. Liu et al. study OPE-model-selection tournaments [ 11 ] , while proxy-assisted best-arm methods use correlated predictions as controls [ 14 ] . RAVEL is not a generic new tournament: it focuses on a world-model residual/occupancy bound and whether matched errors reduce audit variance. Surrogate methods also require true-data certification [ 13 ] . Relative error. Bhamidipaty et al. characterize ordinal inversions in imperfect world models [ 2 ] .
